questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note describes a study where participants are told the true purpose after completion. What is this called?
questions.explanation: Debriefing is post-study disclosure of purpose and findings. It differs from consent, randomization, and blinding, which occur before or during the study.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note flags a study that registered hypotheses before data collection. Why does this matter?

options.text: It prevents changing hypotheses after seeing data
It removes the need for ethics review

questions.explanation: Preregistration locks hypotheses and analysis plans before data collection, reducing HARKing and p-hacking. It does not ensure significance or replace ethics review.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note describes verifying that an experimental condition actually changed the intended variable. What is this?
questions.explanation: A manipulation check verifies the independent variable had its intended effect. Power analysis, reliability, and confound control address different questions.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note reveals exclusions were chosen after seeing the data. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: Post-hoc exclusions can be tuned to produce desired results, inflating false positives. Pre-specified rules protect validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note shows a review citing only studies supporting one view. What is this?
questions.explanation: Citing only supportive studies is cherry-picking, which biases conclusions. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses aim for comprehensive inclusion.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note quotes a finding without attribution. What is the issue?

options.text: It is always acceptable in notes

questions.explanation: Unattributed quotes risk plagiarism and misattribution. Proper citation preserves credit and allows verification.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Why is debriefing especially important after deception?

answer.exemplar: Debriefing restores trust and corrects misconceptions by revealing the true purpose and removing any false beliefs created during the study.

questions.explanation: Deception can leave participants misinformed or distressed. Debriefing corrects this and maintains ethical standards and trust.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note compares a new therapy to untreated patients from 20 years ago. What is the concern?

options.text: Historical groups are identical to current ones
Historical data are always more accurate

questions.explanation: Historical baselines may differ in care, populations, and measurement over time, confounding comparisons. Concurrent controls are preferred.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Compare an observed effect to a threshold
questions.stem: A clinician's note reports a 6-point improvement; the clinically important threshold is 10 points. How many points short is it?
questions.explanation: Subtract 6 from 10 to get 4 points short of the threshold. The effect is real but below the clinically important level.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a breach of participant agreement
questions.stem: A clinician's note says data promised confidential were later published with identifiers. What occurred?

options.text: A breach of the participation agreement

questions.explanation: Publishing identifiable data after promising confidentiality breaches the agreement and harms participants. It is not minor, acceptable, or standard.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: What should a thorough debriefing include?
questions.explanation: A thorough debriefing explains purpose, procedures, and results and answers questions. It does not merely thank, demand secrecy, or recruit.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish preregistration from registration of trials
questions.stem: How does preregistration of analysis plans differ from trial registration?

options.text: Preregistration specifies hypotheses and analyses before data

questions.explanation: Preregistration details hypotheses and analyses in advance. Trial registration records study existence; both matter but serve different roles.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note reports the manipulation check failed. What follows?

options.text: Proceed as if the manipulation worked
Interpret treatment effects cautiously or not at all

questions.explanation: If the manipulation failed, treatment effects are uninterpretable. Adjusting alpha or dropping controls does not fix the problem.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Recommend a safeguard against post-hoc exclusions
questions.stem: What safeguard reduces risk from post-hoc exclusions?
questions.explanation: Pre-registered exclusion criteria prevent selective removal. Post-hoc or hidden exclusions threaten validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

stimulus.body: A review graph shows 12 positive studies and 0 negative or null studies on a popular therapy, with no mention of unpublished trials.

questions.stem: What is the most likely problem?

options.text: Publication bias may distort the review

questions.explanation: An absence of negative or null studies suggests publication bias. Effectiveness cannot be assumed from a one-sided literature base.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: When must a source be cited in a research report?

options.text: For ideas, data, or claims from others

questions.explanation: Citation is needed for others' ideas, data, and claims, not just direct quotes. Common knowledge is a narrow exception, and citations belong throughout.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: When is deception in research ethically justified?

options.text: When no alternative exists and risk is minimal with debriefing

questions.explanation: Deception requires scientific necessity, minimal risk, and thorough debriefing. Convenience, payment, or interest do not justify it.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a difference from a historical baseline
questions.stem: A clinician's note compares a new program's mean of 84 to a historical mean of 76. What is the difference?
questions.explanation: Subtract 76 from 84 to get 8. The raw difference ignores secular changes and noncomparability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Interpret an effect relative to a minimal important difference
questions.stem: An effect of 3 points is observed; the minimal important difference is 5. What is the conclusion?

options.text: The effect is below the important threshold

questions.explanation: An effect smaller than the minimal important difference is not practically important, regardless of statistical significance.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a remedy for a breach
questions.stem: After inadvertently disclosing participant data, what is the best immediate step?

options.text: Notify affected participants and the ethics board

questions.explanation: Transparency and notification allow mitigation and oversight. Concealment, deletion, or distraction worsen harm and violate ethics.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Why should debriefing occur promptly after participation?

answer.exemplar: Prompt debriefing corrects misconceptions while memory is fresh, reduces distress, and prevents participants from leaving with false beliefs.

questions.explanation: Delaying debriefing lets misconceptions persist and may increase harm. Prompt disclosure protects participants and data quality.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which is a limitation of preregistration?

options.text: It cannot fix a flawed design
It removes the need for review

questions.explanation: Preregistration improves transparency but cannot rescue a poorly designed study. It also does not guarantee replication or replace review.
questions.hint: Planning does not fix design flaws.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish manipulation check from dependent measure
questions.stem: Which item is a manipulation check rather than a dependent measure?

options.text: Rating how stressful the task felt

questions.explanation: A manipulation check verifies the intended experience, such as perceived stress. Exam scores, study hours, and GPA are outcomes, not checks.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate impact of exclusions on sample size
questions.stem: A study starts with 120 participants and excludes 15 after data inspection. How many remain?
questions.explanation: Subtract 15 from 120 to get 105. Post-hoc exclusions reduce sample size and can bias results.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a systematic review from a selective one?
questions.explanation: Systematic reviews use predefined search and inclusion criteria. Selective reviews omit such safeguards and risk bias.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note shows an author reusing their own prior text without citation. What is this?
questions.explanation: Reusing one's own published text without citation is self-plagiarism. Efficiency and clarity do not excuse it.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify when debriefing may be delayed
questions.stem: When might debriefing be delayed rather than immediate?

options.text: When immediate disclosure would ruin a multi-session design

questions.explanation: Debriefing may be delayed if immediate disclosure would compromise a multi-session design, but it must occur as soon as feasible. Forgetfulness, fatigue, or results do not justify delay.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Explain why concurrent controls are preferred
questions.stem: Why are concurrent control groups preferred over historical baselines?

answer.exemplar: Concurrent controls experience the same period, care standards, and measurement, reducing confounding from secular changes and selection differences.

questions.explanation: Historical baselines differ in time, care, and measurement. Concurrent controls share the same context, improving comparability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Compute a ratio to a threshold
questions.stem: An effect of 12 points is observed against a threshold of 8. What is the ratio of effect to threshold?
questions.explanation: Divide 12 by 8 to get 1.5. The effect exceeds the threshold by 50 percent.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify an agreement violation in data sharing
questions.stem: A dataset is shared publicly despite consent limiting use to the original team. What is violated?

options.text: Nothing, open data is always good

questions.explanation: Consent limits define permissible use. Sharing beyond them violates the agreement and participant trust.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: What risk arises if debriefing is omitted after a stressful task?

options.text: Participants may leave distressed and misinformed

questions.explanation: Omitting debriefing can leave participants distressed and misinformed. Statistical outcomes are unaffected by ethics lapses.
questions.hint: Ethics lapses harm participants, not p-values.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which should be specified in a preregistration?
questions.explanation: Preregistration should specify hypotheses, variables, and analysis plans. Conclusions and identities are inappropriate or impossible to pre-specify.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Why are manipulation checks important for internal validity?

answer.exemplar: They confirm the independent variable actually produced the intended difference, so observed effects can be attributed to the manipulation rather than a failed induction.

questions.explanation: Without verifying the manipulation, a null result may reflect a failed induction rather than no effect. Checks protect internal validity.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: What is a transparent way to handle exclusions?

options.text: Report exclusions and reasons in a flow diagram

questions.explanation: Reporting exclusions and reasons, such as in a CONSORT flow, supports transparency. Silent or outcome-based exclusion undermines trust.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a corrective for selective reviews
questions.stem: What best corrects a selective literature review?
questions.explanation: Including null and negative findings balances the evidence base. Adding only positive or recent studies increases bias.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note paraphrases a source's idea. Must it be cited?

options.text: Yes, the idea still belongs to the source

questions.explanation: Paraphrased ideas require citation. Citation is not limited to verbatim quotes or journal contexts.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a debriefing element after deception
questions.stem: After deception, what must debriefing include?

options.text: Explanation of the deception and its necessity

questions.explanation: Debriefing after deception must explain the deception and why it was necessary. Demands, dismissal, or withholding are unethical.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a threat in historical comparisons
questions.stem: Which threat is most serious in historical baseline comparisons?
questions.explanation: Secular trends and selection differences confound historical comparisons. Measurement error and typos are lesser or unrelated issues.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Explain why thresholds vary by context
questions.stem: Why should thresholds for important effects depend on context?

answer.exemplar: The same numeric change can matter in one setting and not another; thresholds should reflect patient values, costs, and risks rather than a universal cutoff.

questions.explanation: Importance depends on stakeholders, costs, and risks. A fixed threshold ignores context and can mislead decisions.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a preventative for agreement breaches
questions.stem: What best prevents breaches of participant agreements?

options.text: Clear written consent with data-use terms

questions.explanation: Written consent with explicit data-use terms sets clear boundaries. Verbal promises, no consent, or free sharing increase breach risk.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: What is a key goal of debriefing?

options.text: To punish participants for poor performance

questions.explanation: Debriefing aims to educate participants and restore trust. It is not for punishment, secret data collection, or rushing.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A power analysis calls for 64 participants per group and 2 groups. What is the total preregistered N?
questions.explanation: Multiply 64 by 2 to get 128. Preregistering total N supports transparency.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: If a manipulation check shows no difference between conditions, what should be concluded?

options.text: The manipulation did not work as intended

questions.explanation: A failed manipulation check means the induction did not create the intended difference. It does not support the hypothesis or invalidate the dependent measure.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which practice is a questionable research practice?

options.text: Excluding outliers only after seeing they affect results

questions.explanation: Selective exclusion based on outcomes is a questionable research practice. Pre-registration, full reporting, and sharing are good practices.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Why must literature reviews include opposing evidence?

answer.exemplar: Including opposing evidence prevents confirmation bias and gives readers a fair, complete picture of what is and is not known.

questions.explanation: Balanced reviews reduce confirmation bias and support credible conclusions. Omitting opposing evidence misleads readers.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A clinician's note copies a paragraph verbatim without quotation marks or citation. What is this?
questions.explanation: Verbatim copying without quotation marks or citation is plagiarism. Paraphrase, fair use, and scholarship require proper attribution.
questions.hint: Verbatim copying needs quotes and citation.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which debriefing omission is most unethical?

options.text: Not revealing the deception at all

questions.explanation: Failing to reveal deception leaves participants misinformed and violates ethical obligations. Other omissions are minor or not required.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Calculate a percent change from baseline
questions.stem: A new treatment scores 90 versus a historical baseline of 75. What is the percent increase?
questions.explanation: The increase is 15, and 15/75 = 0.20, or 20 percent. Historical comparisons still need caution.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Identify when an effect meets a threshold
questions.stem: An effect of 8 points is observed with a threshold of 5. What is the conclusion?
questions.explanation: An effect of 8 exceeds a threshold of 5, so it meets the importance criterion. It is not zero and the threshold remains meaningful.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: A researcher uses participant data for a new purpose not covered by consent. What is this?

options.text: A violation of the use agreement

questions.explanation: Using data beyond consented purposes violates the use agreement and participant trust. Efficiency or standard practice do not excuse it.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS

stimulus.body: A note shows participants completed a stressful task and were debriefed three weeks later by email.

questions.stem: What is the concern with this debriefing?

options.text: The delay is too long for effective debriefing

questions.explanation: A three-week delay is too long; debriefing should be prompt. Email may be acceptable, but timing is the main problem.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a benefit of preregistration for reproducibility
questions.stem: How does preregistration support reproducibility?

answer.exemplar: By documenting hypotheses and analyses in advance, preregistration lets others see exactly what was planned, making it easier to replicate and detect deviations.

questions.explanation: Clear advance plans reduce ambiguity and selective reporting, aiding replication and transparency.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify when a manipulation check is unnecessary
questions.stem: When is a manipulation check least necessary?

options.text: When the manipulation is novel and subtle
When the manipulation is obvious and verified by design

questions.explanation: Obvious, design-verified manipulations need less checking. Novel, subtle, subjective, or small-sample cases benefit from checks.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which exclusion is least questionable?

options.text: Excluding participants whose removal makes results significant
Excluding participants who failed an attention check pre-specified in the plan

questions.explanation: Pre-specified attention-check exclusions are legitimate. Outcome-driven, post-hoc, or demographic exclusions are questionable.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a sign of selective citation

stimulus.body: A review's reference list shows 20 studies, all with positive results, and none with null or negative findings on the same topic.

questions.stem: What does this pattern suggest?

options.text: The topic has no negative studies

questions.explanation: An all-positive reference list suggests selective citation or publication bias. Comprehensive reviews include mixed findings.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: Which citation practice is an error?

options.text: Citing the original source of an idea
Citing a source you did not read

questions.explanation: Citing unread sources can propagate errors. Reading and citing original sources is preferred.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.stem: When should debriefing occur in a deception study with multiple sessions?

options.text: Only after the final session if earlier disclosure would compromise the design

questions.explanation: Debriefing should be delayed only when necessary for design integrity and provided as soon as feasible. Withholding entirely, early disclosure, or conditional debriefing are wrong.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a way to improve historical comparisons
questions.stem: How can a historical comparison be strengthened?

options.text: Use a larger historical sample only
Adjust for known differences and use concurrent controls when possible

questions.explanation: Adjusting for known differences and preferring concurrent controls reduces confounding. Larger samples or ignoring time do not fix comparability.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.topic: Judging an effect against a threshold
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a confidence interval helps threshold judgment
questions.stem: Why does a confidence interval help when judging an effect against a threshold?

answer.exemplar: A confidence interval shows whether the entire plausible range exceeds or falls below the threshold, preventing overconfidence from a single point estimate.

questions.explanation: Intervals reveal uncertainty around the estimate. If the interval crosses the threshold, the effect's importance is uncertain.

provenance.author: bank-team-research-methods
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: RESEARCH_METHODS
questions.learningObjective: Identify a consent violation in recruitment
questions.stem: A researcher pressures employees to participate by implying job consequences. What is violated?

options.text: Voluntary participation and the consent agreement

questions.explanation: Coercion violates voluntary participation and the consent agreement. Adulthood does not make participation voluntary under pressure.
